3.2 Analysis
The improved subjective accuracy performance over the
baseline method (our most notable result) appears to be a
consequence of our additional brain-aligned optimization in-
ference process. By using a brain encoding model without
any pre-training to bias the feature extraction process, our
optimization target is trained to be sensitive to the same fea-
tures as the brain. This builds an intuition for why human
raters prefer these images, as presumably, their brains are
utilizing similar features to perform their subjective evalu-
ation. Future work could further examine this relationship,
exploring whether brain encoding models truly produce em-
beddings that better approximate human subjective evalua-
tions.
The trajectory of the brain correlation scores over the var-
ious stages of the reconstruction pipeline sheds some in-
sights into how our refinement process affects representa-
tions in visual cortex. Examining Figure 6, early visual ar-
eas such as V1-V4 have a steeper rate of convergence over
the search process, which makes sense given that our brain-
optimized inference process refines only low-level features
through the updating of the latent z vector. Higher visual ar-
eas, by contrast, improve substantially but at a slower rate.
The largest improvements in feature metrics over the base
decoding method were also found in high-level image met-
rics, so there appears to also be a clear improvement in the
semantic accuracy of the reconstructions. One reason for
this could be the specification of a smaller family of images
within a CLIP space. Any given CLIP vector can describe a
family of images with varying semantic accuracy with re-
spect to the ground truth image, but by selecting images
within that space that score well across visual cortex, we
narrow the space to contain only images that have a closer
semantic relation with the measured brain activity, and by
extension the target image.
Figure 6: Correlation between predicted and actual brain ac-
tivity (y-axis) for the images at each iteration (x-axis) for
different ROIs (curves). For samples that meet the variance
target at earlier iterations, the scores from their latest itera-
tions are carried forward and represented in future iterations
to avoid a sample bias in the plot.
Figure 7 examines the rate at which brain areas reach their
target variance threshold, used as our stopping criterion dur-
ing the BOI algorithm. The percentage of samples that reach
this threshold steadily increases across the hierarchy of vi-
sual processing areas. Interestingly, the rate at which the
samples converge orders brain areas by their level of repre-
sentational invariance, with V1 converging most slowly, fol-
lowed by V2, V3, V4, and higher-level visual cortex, which
aligns with invariance metrics explored in other works, such
as receptive field size (Kay et al. 2013).
Figure 7: Percentage of samples in the test set (n= 982) for
which reconstructions have reached our target variance com-
puted across denoised trial repetitions of the original brain
activity (y-axis), for different ROIs (curves) across iterations
(x-axis). The target variance for the NSD General mask is
used as a stopping criterion during the search, but for this
plot, the target variance is computed individually for each
brain area.
4 Limitations
For the technical limitations of our implementation, the most
immediate limitation lies in the computational cost of re-
peatedly sampling images from a diffusion model. This ad-
ditional inference stage increases the required number of
GPU cycles by an order of magnitude relative to the base
decoding model. This could be improved with faster image
generation models, but will always represent an increase in
GPU cycles over direct decoding approaches, as it requires
generating many intermediate images in addition to the final
image distribution.
This method also does not have a way to verify the accu-
racy of the stopping criterion used during the search process.
A stopping criterion is necessary to avoid overfitting to the
encoding model and our averaged brain activity target, but
when representing a distribution, a meaningful measurement
of distribution width corresponding to perceptual certainty is
also desirable. Our current approach is likely an incomplete
solution to many of these objectives, as the autoencoder re-
moves a lot of brain noise that is relevant to quantifying
an appropriate estimate of neural uncertainty. Because the
encoding model produces noise-free β′s, the motivation for
implementing the autoencoder was to create a mechanism
for translating between the encoded beta variance σ(β′) and
the measured beta variance σ(β), which is larger by approx-
imately two orders of magnitude. A more robust and well-
motivated stopping criterion would be rich ground for fu-
ture work, providing a more convincing estimate of the ob-
server’s perceptual uncertainty in the represented image dis-
tribution.
5 Conclusion
We introduce a procedure for optimizing fMRI image recon-
structions against a brain correlation metric while simulta-
neously reducing the breadth of the decoded image distribu-
tions to align with brain variance across denoised trial repe-
titions. We find that this procedure generates high-quality re-
constructions and improves performance across a variety of
feature spaces without performing any additional optimiza-
tion in any of them. A key component of our system is our
use of brain-optimized encoding models that yield accurate
predictions of brain activity in much of visual cortex (St-
Yves et al. 2022), allowing us to leverage the diversity of
representations for natural images across visual cortex. The
potential of this tool for deeper analysis is also demonstrated
in quantifying the invariance in representations across the
brain via each brain area’s rate of convergence to our stop-
ping criterion. We find that our method sorts brain areas
in agreement with complementary measures of invariance
explored in other works. By utilizing encoding models to
align reconstructions directly with the measured brain activ-
ity, this work aims to expand work in this space to utilize the
more descriptive and complete objective of brain correlation,
allowing these tools to give new insights into the structure
and function of various cortical regions. We believe image
reconstruction algorithms have a pivotal role to play in un-
derstanding and interpreting brain activity in visual cortex,
and reconstructing complex perceptual states.

### SOURCE: Resonant_leaky_modes_in_all-dielectric_metasystems_Fundamentals_and_applications_f036f530ca.pdf ###
Resonant leaky modes in all-dielectric metasystems: Fundamentals 
and Applications 
Lujun Huang1,2, Lei Xu3, David Powell1, Willie Padilla4, Andrey E Miroshnichenko1* 
1. School of Engineering and Information Technologies, University of New South Wales, 
Canberra, ACT, 2600, Australia 
2. School of Physics and Electronic Science, East China Normal University, Shanghai, 200241, 
China   
3. Advanced Optics and Photonics Laboratory, Department of Engineering, School of 
Science and Technology, Nottingham Trent University, Nottingham NG11 8NS, United 
Kingdom 
4. Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Duke University, Durham, North 
Carolina 27705, USA 
Corresponding author: andrey.miroshnichenko@unsw.edu.au 
 
All-dielectric metamaterials and metasurfaces have been demonstrated as ideal platform s to manipulate 
electromagnetic waves and enhance light-matter interaction. Analogous to guided modes in a dielectric 
waveguide, high refractive index dielectric metasurface supports leaky modes (also known as 
quasi-normal modes ), including electric and magnetic resonant modes, which are represented by a 
complex eigenfrequency. Such leaky modes play a dominant role in governing the optical properties of 
dielectric nanoparticles and metasurfaces (i.e., absorption, scattering and emission ). Th ese unique 
properties enable researchers to design dielectric metasurface s with desired functionalities without 
resorting to computationally expensive parameter scanning with full-wave simulation. Moreover, leaky 
modes underpin many exciting topics, such as Fano resonance s, bound sta tes in the continuum (leaky 
modes with Q=+ ), coherent perfect absor ption, parity -time symmetry, and exceptional points. This 
review provides an overview of the recent progress on leaky modes of all -dielectric-based metasystem, 
from fundamental physics to their applications. We start with surveying the fundamental physics of 
leaky modes and discussing leaky mode engineering in either a passive or active way. Then, we discuss 
the recent progress on  the leaky modes ’ application in  the perfect light absorber, solar cell s, 
photodetectors, enhanced light emission and lasing, strong coupling, enhanced nonlinear harmonic 
generation, and structural color. Next, we present an overview of recent advances in bound states in the 
continuum and their application in enhanced light-matter interactions. Also, we review other interesting 
topics: parity-time symmetry and exceptional points, and discuss their application in manipulating light 
in an unprecedented way. Finally, we present our vision of the challenges and opportunities in t his 
rapidly developing field of research.
1. Introduction 
In 1908, Gustav Mie  derived the analytical solu tion of a single dielectric particle made of 
high-index semiconductors  with regular shape s like two -dimensional (2D) cylinder s and 
three-dimensional (3D) sphere s by solving Maxwell equation s1–3. He found a  series of resonant 
peaks in the absorption and scattering cross-section spectrum, which are termed as Mie resonance 
to recognize his outstanding contributions to optics and photonics . Thanks to the significant 
advancement of modern nanofabrication technology, Mie resonance has been reinvigorated in the 
past two decades and found great success in controlling and manipulating light in an 
unprecedented way. Similar to metallic nanostructu res supporting plasmonic resonances, 
high-index dielectric nanostructures support multi polar electric and magnetic Mie resonances , 
providing much freedom to control the light -matter interaction at a subwavelength scale. Besides, 
they ha ve much lower losses compared to noble metals like silver and gold. These two 
extraordinary properties enable researchers to develop high -performance nanophotonic devices, 
such as metalens, low -threshold nanolasers, light-emitting diodes, solar cells, and photodetectors. 
The rich library of dielectrics, including Si, Ge, GaAs, AlGaAs, GaN, TiO2, and Si3N4, allows 
researchers and scientists to desi gn these photonic devices operating from ultraviolet, visible, 
near-infrared, mid -infrared to terahertz wavelength range . Moreover, all -dielectric metasystems, 
particularly all -silicon metasurface, are compatible with CMOS fabrication processes , making it 
possible to develop integrated photonic circuits. In the past decade, there have been many excellent 
reviews on all -dielectric metamaterials and metasurface 4,5,14–16,6–13, which cover  either wavefront 
manipulation or Mie-resonance enhanced light-matter interactions.  
Essentially, each Mie resonance in the dielectric structure s can be perfectly linked with an 
eigenmode, also named a leaky mode or quasi -normal mode (QNM)17,18. It has been demonstrated 
that the leaky modes provided by a single  or an array of dielectric nanoparticles (NPs) govern the 
optical properties (i.e., scattering /absorption) of structures.  Note that  dielectric structures are not 
the only platform to support leaky modes or QNMs. Generally speaking, leaky modes exist in any 
open non -Hermitian systems , including  but not limited to  plasmonic NPs and metasurface s, 
dielectric NPs and metasurface s, coupled ring or disk resonators and waveguides  as long as they 
interact with exterior environment . It has been well established in the text book of quantum 
mechanics that Hermitian Hamiltonians give rise to the real eigenvalue s or eigen -energies and 
orthogonal eigen-basis. However, the boundary condition in many photonic and acoustic systems 
like metasurfaces are open at least in one dimension. Consequently, their Hamiltonians are 
non-Hermitian, leading to the complex eigenvalues of eigenmodes  that are the typical features of 
leaky modes. As a particular type of leaky modes with an infinite quality-factor (Q-factor), bound 
states in the continuum  (BICs) have attracted considerable attentions in both fundamental physics 
and practical applications. Besides,  many other interesting physics and applications related to 
non-Hermitian photonics,  such as parity-time (PT) symmetry and exceptional points (EPs), have 
been explored and demonstr ated by tailoring the loss and gain of  the system. The fundamental 
physics behind the m can be attributed to the leaky modes engineering. Given the importance  and 
powerful capabilities of the leaky modes, we review the all -dielectric metasystem from the leaky 
modes’ perspective. In section 2, w e first discuss the  fundamental physics behind  leaky modes , 
including the definition and calculation of leaky modes, and then  reveal the vital ro le of leaky 
modes played in dictating the optical properties of all -dielectric metastructures from temporal
coupled-mode theory  (CMT). After verifying the key role  of leaky modes, we  discuss several 
methods of engineering leaky modes. Then, we present an overview of leaky mode applications in 
perfect light absorption, solar cell s, photodetectors, enhanced light emission and lasing, strong 
coupling, enhanced nonlinear ha rmonic generation, and structural  color. In section 3, we rev iew 
the most recent progress of BICs  which are special leaky modes with an infinite Q-factor, 
including the fundamental physics behind BICs and their applications in enhanced light -matter 
interactions. In section 4, as the byproduct of leaky mode coupling, we survey the recen t advances 
of PT-symmetry and EPs and their applications in laser s, laser -coherent perfect absorber s, and 
sensors. Section 5 concludes and presents an outlook of challenges and potential opportunities  in 
all-dielectric nanophotonics.        
       
 
Fig.1. Resonant leaky modes  can be linked to many interesting topics, including Mie resonances, BICs /QBICs, 
PT-symmetry and EPs in an open all-dielectric metasystem.  
 
2. Leaky modes in all-dielectric structures and their applications 
A non-hermitian system support s a series of leaky modes or QNMs because it strongly interact s 
with the exterior enviro nment due to the open boundary. Typical examples include a single or an 
array of metallic or dielectric structures, or hybrid dielectric -metallic systems. This work mainly 
focuses on the all-dielectric structure, as shown in Fig.2.  
 
Before we start discussing leaky modes, it is necessary to revisit the concept of guided modes, 
which share some similar features with leaky modes but have totally different phy sics and 
applications. We use a multilayer slab structure as an example to illustrate the diffe rence between 
guided modes  and leaky mod es (See Fig. 3a-b). Guided modes are  sustained only when the 
refractive index of the core layer is larger than the top and bottom layer  (n2>n1 in Fig.3). Assuming 
the top and bottom layers have the same refractive indices, then eigenfunction in the core layer is a 
propagating wave while it shows exponential decay in the upper and down regions. The dispersion 
relationship can be obtained analytically by solving the Maxwell  equation, which has been
explicitly discussed in many text books, see  Yariv et al 19. Fig. 3e shows a typical eigenfield 
distribution inside and outside the waveguide region. It is clearly seen that outside the high -index 
core layer the eigenfield decays exponentially to zero i n the far -field while it satisfies  sine or 
cosine function inside the core layer  depending on the parity of the guided modes. The formation 
of guided modes in such a structure can be explained intuitively from geometry optics perspective. 
The eigenfield inside the core layer can be represented by a superposition of two plane waves. One 
can be regarded as the incident wave while the other is the reflected wave. The incident wave 
experiences total internal reflection at the interface due to n 2>n1, ensuring the field confinement 
inside the core layer. However, only  satisfying the total internal reflection does not gurantee the 
formation of guided modes. The accumulated phase in a round trip must be an integral multiple of 
2. This unique perspective remind s us that guided modes shall be excited by the endfire coupling 
at the end of the waveguide. One may use a similar way to explain the formation of guided modes 
in the cylindrical waveguide , as schematically shown in Fig. 3c. The only difference is that the 
eigenfields inside and outside the core layer are Bessel functions. More detailed discussions can be 
found in the text books19, and we shall not repeat them here.  
 
Unlike the guided modes, the eigenfields of leaky modes outside the hig h-index core layer 
propagates to  infinity instead of de caying exponentially in the far -field (see Fig.3 f). For the 
multilayer slab structure in Fig. 3b, the eigenfrequencies and eigenfields  of leaky modes  can be 
solved analytically , as discussed in the following section . A leaky mode is characterized by a 
complex eigenfrequency =0-i, where 0 and  are the resonant frequency and radiative decay 
rate of leaky modes, respectively. Its eigenfield should satisfy the out-going boundary condition so 
that the energy leaks out from resonators. It  also shows divergence at r→ due to its complex 
eigenfrequencies, as confirmed in Fig.3f . Since the eigenfields are propagating wave in the 
far-field, according to the reciprocal theorem these leaky modes can be excited by an external 
source (i.e., plane wave or structured beam). Under such circumstances, the total internal reflection 
is no longer satisfied.  A similar analysis also works for leaky modes in a  single circular wire, as 
schematically shown in Fig.3d. Thus, we can conclude that the same structure can support  both 
guided modes and leaky modes. However, the excitation method is different for guided modes and 
leaky modes due to the different formation mechanisms. As a result, they cannot be excited 
simultaneously, and only one can be excited by the corresponding excita tion way. Another way to 
distinguish guided modes and leaky modes is to check whether the dispersion relationship is below 
or above the light cone because the guided (leaky) mode is below (above) the light cone. This 
section reviews the fundamental physics of leaky modes in all-dielectric metastructures and their 
applications in enhancing light-matter interaction.
Fig.2. Schematic drawing of all-dielectric-based open systems. (a) 1D dielectric slab; (b) 2D dielectric cylinder; (c) 
3D dielectric sphere; (d) all -dielectric metagrating; (e) all -dielectric metasurface made of an array of cuboid 
structures; (f) photonic crystal slab. 
 
 
 
Fig.3. Comparison between guided modes and leaky modes. (a -b) Schematic drawing of guided modes (a) and 
leaky modes (b) in a 1D slab; (c-d) Schematic drawing of guided modes (c) and leaky modes (d) in a 2D dielectric 
cylinder; (e) Eigenfield distribution of the first two guided modes in a 1D slab with n1=1 and n2=4. The thickness 
of the slab is 300nm and the operating wavelength is 1.55 m; (e) Eigenfield distribution of the first and second 
leaky modes in 1D slab with n1=1 and n2=4.
2.1. Definition of leaky modes and coupled-mode theory 
2.1.1 Leaky modes in dielectric structures

1D slab (Fig. 4a), 2D circular wire (Fig. 4d) and 3D sphere (Fig. 4h) because both complex 
eigenfrequency and eigenfield of their leaky modes can be solved analytically with Mie -theory by 
boundary matching condition or scattering pole approach20–22 (See Appendix-A for detailed derivation).

Except for the complex eigenfrequencies, their eigenfields can be calculated accordingly. One may find 
detailed derivations in Appendix. Note that the complex eigenfrequency calculated from Eqs.  (1)-(3) is 
represented by =0-i, where 0 and  are the resonant frequency and radiative decay rate of leaky 
modes, respectively. To make the applications of leaky modes as general as possible, we define the 
normalized complex eigenvalue N=Nreal+1i*Nimag=n2ka=n2a/c, where n2 is the refractive index of 
dielectric structure, a is the feature size of the geometry (i.e., a=L for slab and a=r0 for 2D ci rcular 
wire and 3D sphere) and c is the speed of light in the free space. Due to their unique shapes, the leaky 
modes have different definitions. For 1D slab, leaky modes are named as TEMm, where m is the number 
of antinodes. For both 2D circular wire and 3D sphere, leaky modes are noted as TEml (or TMml), where 
m is the azimuthal mode number and l is the radial order number. Without loss of generality, we set the 
refractive index of the background medium and dielectric structure as n 1=1 and n2=4, respectively. Figs. 
4b, 4e, 4i show some leaky modes’ complex eigenvalues in a 1D slab, 2D circular wire and 3D  sphere. 
Additionally, we also plot the eigenfield -distributions of several leaky modes as examples to illustrate 
the definition of eigenmodes, as shown in Fig s. 4c, 4f-g and 4i-j. The complex eigenvalues of leaky 
modes show an interesting dependence on the refractive index. From Fig.5, it could be easily found that 
the imaginary parts of leaky modes are quite sensitive to the refractive index of dielectric resonators.
Nevertheless, their real parts are almost unchanged with the varied index. The stable real parts c an be 
intuitively understood by the resonant condition 𝑛2𝑘𝐿 = 𝑚𝜋. The large vari ation on the imaginary 
parts can be attributed to the reduced index contrast between dielectrics and background medium, 
which is air here.  
   
For a single or several dielectric particles with irregular shapes, their eigenmode information could be 
obtained with either numerical methods like the resonant-state expansion method or commercial 
software COMSOL MULTIPHYSICS.  In the case of an array of dielectric structures, their leaky 
modes are usually calculated by numerical methods or commercial software . However, there are still  
some theor etical works sh owing that the leaky modes could be solved in a semi -analytical way 23–26, 
including the resonant-state expansion method 26. In the next part, we discuss the numerical methods 
that have been developed for calculating the leaky modes in all-dielectric resonators.

2.1.2 Temporal Coupled Mode Theory  
The powerful capability of leaky modes is that they play a dominant role in governing the optical 
properties (i.e., scattering, reflection/transmission and absorption) of dielectric structures 20,21,27–30, 
which is manifested by the temporal coupled -mode theory (CMT). Generally speaking, temporal CMT 
treats the structure as an optical resonator, and describes the optical response of the structure in terms 
of coupling between the incident wave and resonant modes supported by the structure. In the past three 
decades, temporal CM T has been successfully applied in describing  the scattering (reflection, 
transmission) and absorption in both plasmonic and dielectric  nanostructures. Here, we first review the 
application of temporal CMT in modelling the optical properties from a single or an array of NPs.  
Case 1: Temporal CMT in a single NP

first kind of Hankel function. Consider ing the TM (H//z) incidence as an example, the total m agnetic 
field outside the structure could be expressed as2,31

asymmetric lineshape in reflection or transmission spectrum 29. For a slab with intrinsic loss, it is not 
difficult to derive the absorption efficiency of a single mode based on temporal CMT, which has the

𝐴 =

From the above equation, it can be easily observed that absorption of a single resonance reaches its 
maximum 50% when intrinsic absorption rate is balanced by the radiation decay rate at resonant 
frequency37, corresponding to the critical coupling conditions. If the single resonance  is supported by a 
layer of infinitesimal thickness, then the resonance must be of even symmetry 37. Otherwise, a relatively 
thick layer ( 𝑡~𝜆/2) may support both even (electric) and odd (magnetic) single resonances. The 
absorption could be enhanced to unity by placing a conductor clos ely behind the lossy slab at a specific 
distance to create an additional resonance of odd symmetry. In this scenario the even mode and odd 
mode each contribute 50% ab sorption, bringing about 100% total absorption. Another approach is to 
use a single structure, e.g. an all -dielectric metasurface, which supports two degenerate modes of 
opposite symmetry with identical resonant frequencies and matched material and radiative decay rates 38. 
On the other hand, perfect coherent absorption may be realized through in -phase (even mode), or 
out-of-phase (odd mode), illumination from two sides, and simultaneous satisfaction of the critical 
coupling condition on resonance. Since a coherent absorber  is either even or odd, it absorbs 100% of 
the incident coherent radiation or, equivalently, 50% of incoherent radiation39. These three strategies of 
electromagnetic wave absorption will be discussed in a later sub -section. Note that Eqs. (16) -(18) only 
strictly apply to a photonic crystal slab or metasurface which is embedded in a symmetric envir onment. 
Asymmetric configurations, with respect to the middle -plane of the layer, are considered by Wang et 
al40.    
In summary, temporal CMT perfectly correlates the  absorption and scattering cros s-section in a single 
2D and 3D structure, or reflection (transmission) and absorption with a complex eigenfrequency of 
resonant mode. The powerful capability of temporal CMT  has been confirmed in many works. Fig. 6 
shows several examples of temporal CMT used for reproducing either the absorption or reflection in a 
single dielectric nanostructure an d photonic crystal slab. Here, it is noteworthy that the total absorption 
could be calculated by summing up the absorption from all leaky modes because absorption only 
depends on the eigenmode information, but does not involve the phase ar ising from backgr ound
scattering. With the information of  the complex eigenvalue of leaky modes in Fig . 4, Yu et al . 
successfully reconstructed the total absorption spectrum of a continuous slab, a single cylinder and a 
sphere20 (Fig.6b), showing a nice agreement with the analytical solutions based on Mie theory. 
Reproducing the scattering matrix of a single, array of dielectric NPs and photonic crystal slab 
becomes complicated and challenging as it requ ires both complex eigenfrequency and scattering from 
the direct transport process. Alpeggiani et al . revealed that reflection and transmission could be 
retrieved by taking account of complex eigenfrequencies and far -field information of all relevant leaky 
modes30 (Fig.6c-d). The scattering cross -section from a single dielectric cylinder and sphere is tackled 
with temporal CMT by Yu et a .l21, where the background reflection phase  is derived analytically. The 
relevant result is presented in Fig. 6e. For a n NP with an irregular shape, Yan et al . found that both 
leaky modes (or QNMs) and perfectly matched layer  modes have to be considered to reproduce the 
scattering and absorption cross -section41. Perfectly matched layer  modes are particular ly important for 
a metal lic NP on the semiconductor substrate. Since this review focuses on the leaky modes in an 
all-dielectric structure, leaky modes in a plasmonic resonator or hybrid plasmonic -dielectric resonator 
are beyond the scope of this review. Readers may refer to two comprehensive reviews written by 
Lalanne et al .17 and Kristensen et al .18, respectively. Before ending the discussion of this section, we 
would like to reiterate that temporal CMT has demonstrated its powerful capability in predicting some 
interesting phenomena like antireflection coating layer42, superscattering32,34, and complete polarization 
conversion43,44. They also enable the design of high -performance photonic and optoel ectronic devices, 
such as solar cells and photodetectors, which are discussed in the later section.

2.2. Numerical methods for calculating leaky modes 
For an open resonator  with regular  geometries such as spheres 20,45, cylinder20, or Fabry -Perot 
resonators17, solutions for scattered fields are available in closed form  (See Appendix -A), which can 
readily be adapted to find modes. However, in practice more complex geometries are of interest, so 
numerical methods must usually be applied. In open systems, with radiation boundary conditions, 
Maxwell’s equations become non -Hermitian. The most important consequence  of this is that the modal 
fields no longer satisfy the usual orthogonality relationships. The eigenfrequencies are complex, 𝜔𝑛 =
𝜔𝑛
′ − 𝑖𝜔𝑛′′, with the imaginary part of passive objects occurring at 𝜔𝑛
′′ < 0 when using the time 
convention exp(−𝑖𝜔𝑡) . Sommerfeld radiation conditions dictate that solutions in the far -field decay 
as exp(𝑖𝑘𝑟) /4𝜋𝑟, with 𝑘 = 𝑘′ − 𝑖𝑘′′ = 𝜔/𝑐. Since 𝑘′′ < 0, this le ads to solutions whic h grow 
exponentially in the far-field. Although this result is initially counter -intuitive, it should be recalled that 
larger values of 𝑟, correspond to earlier values in time when the energy was radiated by the source. 
Since at the c omplex eigenfrequency the source strength diverges as 𝑡 → −∞, the corresponding 
radiated fields must also diverge as 𝑟 → ∞. Further discussion of causality and convergence can be 
found in Ref  46. This divergence means that the usual ortho -normality conditions do not apply, since 
they correspond to normalization of the energy in the field, which is unbounded. Instead, they satisfy a 
bi-orthogonality relationship with a set of adjoint modes, under an unconjugated inner product 47. This 
unconventional normalization is what gives rise to the term QNMs. 
 
2.2.1 Semi-analytical approaches 
A review of early work on QNMs can be found in Ref  48. Initial techniques for studying open systems 
were based on the “system and bath” approach. Here, the problem is partitio ned into two parts, the 
modes of which are solved separately,  and then coupled together. The system (e.g. the internal part of 
the cavity, or the body of the dielectric resonator) is solved with closed boundaries, giving a discrete set 
of normal modes. The  surrounding bath (e.g. free space) has a continuous spectrum of modes. This 
approach is in principle generally applicable, however in some cases the division between the system 
and the bath can be difficult, and the resulting formulation requires dealing with a continuous modal 
spectrum. QNMs are introduced as a more intuitive approach, allowing analysis to be performed with 
only a finite set of discrete modes of the entire system, enabling established techniques for closed 
systems to be applied to open resonators. 
A contemporary, semi-analytical approach to finding QNMs is known as the resonant-state expansion26. 
This approach starts with the eigen-solutions to a known scattering problem, such as a dielectric sphere, 
and applies perturbation theory to find the solution for other geometries. This approach has been used 
to demonstrate quasi-BICs (QBICs) for dielect ric resonators 49 and their applications to nonlinear 
nanophotonics50. The main drawback of this approach is the complexity of constructing the required 
perturbation matrices and the difficulty of incorporating background media other than free space, such 
as a substrate. 
 
2.2.2 Boundary element approaches
Boundary element approaches are advantageous for open resonator problems since they solve only for 
the fields on the surface of the object (or equivalent surface currents). These fields remain finite at 
complex frequencies, thus they require no special tre atment of diverging solutions. For metallic objects 
at microwave frequencies, which are treated as perfect electric conductors, this approach was originally 
referred to as the singularity expansion method and was primarily motivated by predicting time-domain 
features of a radar echo based on the resonant modes of a target51. 
 
For dielectric objects, initial approaches have been suggested based on finding the minimum of the 
condition number or determinant of the system matrix 52. More recently, integral approaches have been 
extended to plasmonic elements 53,54 (Fig.7a-b), and all -dielectric meta -atoms55(Fig.7c), where it was 
shown that the non -orthogonality of the resonator modes leads to interference between them. This can 
explain certain effects, such as the anapole moments , which lead to the suppression of dipolar radiation. 
Open-source solvers of QNMs based on the boundary element method can be found in Ref 56,57. 
In boundary element approaches, the system matrix always includes terms with high -order frequency 
dependence, thus regular eigenvalue solvers cannot be used to find the modes. Instead, iterative 
methods or contour integration must be used 58,59. This means that no special approach is req uired to 
deal with dispersive media, so long as their model can be continued analytically in the complex 
frequency domain (e.g. with a Drude -Lorentz model). For all numerical methods, it is important to 
distinguish between physically meaningful resonances of the structure, and purely numerical solutions 
introduced by the discrete operator. Appropriate choice of the integral operator can ensure that the 
unwanted numerical solutions are well separated from the true solutions in complex frequency space.  
In many practical problems, the background medium of a nanoresonator is not free space. Instead , it 
may be located on a substrate (possibly with multiple layers), embedded within a waveguide, or placed 
within a more complex structure such as a photonic crystal. In such cases, it is necessary to use a more 
complex Green’s function, which may not be available in closed form. Since some other numerical 
method, such as finite element , may be needed to find such Green’s functions, in many cases it is 
simpler to use this method to directly solve for the QNMs. 
 
2.2.3 Finite element approaches 
Finite element methods (FEM) are often favoured in numerical solution of electromagnetic problems, 
due to their highly flexible mesh, and suitability to problems and geometries of almost arbitrary 
complexity. Since they require discretization of the entire  computational domain, radiation conditions 
must be explicitly enforced at boundaries using techniques such as perfectly matched layers. The 
incorporation of such boundary conditions into an eigenvalue solver is one of the main complexities of 
using FEM to  find QNMs. It has been shown that the normalization can be performed using only a 
volume integral over the entire computational domain, including the perfectly matched layer. This was 
used to calculate the Purcell factor for open optical resonators 60, where traditional methods typically 
fail due to the mode volume becoming unbounded. 
One advantage of FEM approaches is that they lead to conventional eigenvalue problems in the case of 
non-dispersive media, since the system matri x does not depend on frequency. In many works, the use 
of dispersive media leads to a nonlinear eigenvalue problem. However, by incorporating auxiliary 
variables into the equation (corresponding to local polarization and its temporal derivatives), the 
system of equations becomes second order again. It has been shown that this leads to a conventional 
quadratic eigenvalue problem for

Semantic Dependency in Microservice Architecture
1st Amr S. Abdelfattah

Abstract—Microservices have been a key architectural ap-
proach for over a decade, transforming system design by
promoting decentralization and allowing development teams to
work independently on specific microservices. While loosely
coupled microservices are ideal, dependencies between them are
inevitable. Often, these dependencies go unnoticed by develop-
ment teams. Although syntactic dependencies can be identified,
tracking semantic dependencies — when multiple microservices
share similar logic — poses a greater challenge. As systems
evolve, changes made to one microservice can trigger ripple
effects, jeopardizing system consistency and requiring updates to
dependent services, which increases maintenance and operational
complexity. Effectively tracking different types of dependencies
across microservices is essential for anticipating the impact of
such changes. This paper introduces the Semantic Dependency
Matrix as an instrument to address these challenges from a
semantic perspective. We propose an automated approach to
extract and represent these dependencies and demonstrate its
effectiveness through a case study. This paper takes a step further
by demonstrating the significance of semantic dependencies,
even in cases where there are no direct dependencies between
microservices. It shows that these hidden dependencies can exist
independently of endpoint or data dependencies, revealing critical
connections that might otherwise be overlooked.
Index Terms—microservice, dependency, coupling, semantic
clones, dependency matrix
I. I NTRODUCTION
Microservice architecture has become the mainstream ap-
proach for cloud-native systems due to its modular and elastic
nature and is increasingly vital for managing the complexity
of modern systems [1]. By breaking down the functionalities
of complex systems into smaller, independent, and loosely
coupled units, microservices enable scalability [2]. However,
as these systems grow in complexity and scale, managing the
dependencies between services becomes increasingly challeng-
ing. While microservices are designed to be loosely coupled,
they often exhibit both explicit dependencies—such as direct
endpoint calls—and implicit dependencies, including shared
logic or semantic relationships, which can lead to inconsisten-
cies across the system [3].
Problem Statement. Dependencies in microservices arise
when changes in one part of the system necessitate corre-
sponding changes in another, whether these dependencies are
explicit or implicit. The implicit dependencies, particularly
those arising from shared logic, or semantic clones, are es-
pecially difficult to detect and manage. Semantic clones occur
when two code fragments perform the same function, while the
fragments could be syntactically different [4]. Such clones can
create hidden dependencies across microservices, leading to
maintenance challenges and potential system inconsistencies.
If semantic dependencies go undetected, even small changes
in one service can have ripple effects, leading to functionality
inconsistency and increased maintenance costs [4].
Microservice architectures, with their distributed nature and
component-based structure, complicate the task of identifying
these semantic dependencies. When components within or
across microservices rely on similar logic or shared func-
tionality, a change in one component can affect others in
unpredictable ways. For instance, two microservices may
implement a shared flow to retrieve specific data, and if one
microservice’s implementation is modified without updating
the other, it can lead to inconsistent system behavior. This
scenario is common when microservices rely on a shared flow
but access an endpoint or data source from another microser-
vice or external service to fulfill the process. In such cases,
endpoint and data dependency analysis would fail to capture
the relationship since there is no direct interaction between
the two microservices. However, semantic dependencies effec-
tively reveal this hidden relationship. Without a comprehensive
view of these interactions, identifying such issues becomes
challenging, especially when system documentation fails to
keep up with the evolving complexity of the implementation.
Objective. The objective of this paper is to introduce an au-
tomated method for detecting semantic dependencies between
microservices based on their architectural components. Our
methodology focuses on identifying component-level semantic
relationships between microservices to identify implicit de-
pendencies that could otherwise go unnoticed. It detects se-
mantic clones between components, meaning that a change in
one component necessitates consideration of the other cloned
component. This establishes semantic dependencies between
the microservices containing those cloned components. By au-
tomating the detection of these dependencies from the system
source code, we aim to provide practitioners with a holistic
view of their system’s semantic structure, enabling them to
arXiv:2501.11787v1  [cs.SE]  20 Jan 2025
better manage the risks associated with code inconsistencies
and maintenance. This paper provides a detailed methodology
to achieve semantic dependency detection and visualization,
supported by a case study for evaluation. Additionally, the case
study explores the potential relationship between semantic
dependencies and endpoint and data dependencies, providing a
more comprehensive view of the system and offering multiple
perspectives for further consideration.
Contributions. The following contributions are made:
• An automated methodology for detecting component-based
semantic dependencies between microservices.
• A matrix-based visualization that offers a holistic view of
semantic dependencies across microservices.
• A case study and prototype implementation to evaluate
the methodology using a well-established benchmark for
validation. It showcases the extraction and visualization of
semantic dependencies across microservices.
• An exploration point of the integration and relationships
among endpoint, data, and semantic dependencies, and
providing a holistic perspective on system dependencies.
Paper Organization. The paper is structured as follows:
Section II reviews related work. Section III presents the
proposed methodology and its phases for constructing the
Semantic Dependency Matrix. In Section IV, we demonstrate
the methodology’s implementation on a benchmark system.
Section V elaborates on the methodology’s insights and ad-
dresses threats to validity. Finally, Section VI concludes the
paper and summarizes its key contributions.
II. R ELATED WORK
One of the critical aspects of software development is
identifying and managing code dependencies [5]. While other
studies [4], [6]–[8] have explored methods for detecting se-
mantic clones in software systems, this task is particularly
challenging in microservices-based systems due to the dis-
tributed nature of the architecture. Unlike syntactic clones,
which are code fragments with similar syntax, semantic clones
do not necessarily share the same code structure and can
sometimes be classified as code smells in certain studies [9].
Zhong et al. [10] state in their work that it is difficult
to manage the quality of microservice applications due to
their separated and self-contained nature. Still, it is important
to know how coupled the different microservices are for
development and rework purposes. Apolinario et al. [11] high-
light the operational complexity of microservices, worsened
by limited monitoring tools and disorganized development,
leading to high coupling. Studies [10]–[12] emphasize that
managing dependencies, particularly semantic ones, is crucial
for maintaining loose coupling in microservice applications,
motivating this study.
Most code clone detection methods focus on syntactic
clones since semantic clones are difficult to handle [13].
Semantic clones require a more in-depth analysis to identify
and detect the meaning behind the code and its structure
[14]. Multiple methods are introduced for clone detection as
described in [4], [6], [9]. However, most of them are built
for monolithic systems. Savic et al. [8] proposed a language-
independent approach for monolithic systems, using enriched
concrete syntax trees (eCSTs) to extract semantic dependen-
cies. However, it focuses solely on monolithic architectures,
ignoring microservice systems. In contrast, Zhao et al. [15]
focused on microservices, using Nicad to detect syntactic
clones and a custom tool to analyze cross-service clones,
emphasizing the reasons behind these clones.
Moreover, there are significant shortcomings in tools to
detect semantic dependencies in microservices. In [9], Com-
ponent Call Graphs (CCGs) were introduced as a possible
alternative to Control Flow Graphs (CFGs). A CCG is created
from the CFG of a code base, where the CFG is condensed into
method units so the flow of method calls is shown. The CCG
describes the control flow of the system across components,
including calls within and between microservices. Using CCGs
is much less expensive due to the reduction of low-level
program detail. They utilized the CCGs to identify clones
across microservices-based systems. However, they did not
consider semantic clones under the context of dependencies
or address them in the context of other types of dependencies.
Nevertheless, we utilized their recommended representation
of CCGs to build our methodology accordingly. We provide
a visualization for the holistic view of the semantic depen-
dencies in microservices-based systems while considering the
component structure and interactions.
Additionally, various visualization approaches have been
developed to represent microservice architectures and their
dependencies [16]–[23]. Specifically related to the presented
visualization in this study, Abdelfattah and Cerny [17] focus
on endpoint and data dependencies within microservices-based
systems. They introduced heat maps to visualize these depen-
dencies in a matrix format, creating two matrices: the Endpoint
Dependency Matrix (EDM) and the Data Dependency Matrix
(DDM). These matrices identify which microservices rely
on endpoints from another microservice, and which share
common data entities with each other. In this study, we apply
matrix visualization to our detected semantic dependencies,
and in the discussion, we integrate our findings with their
matrices, offering a comprehensive view that encompasses all
three dependency aspects for further investigation.
This paper presents an automated approach for defining,
extracting, and visualizing semantic dependencies within the
source code of microservices-based systems. It highlights the
significance of recognizing these dependencies for effective
system maintainability.
III. C OMPONENT -BASED SEMANTIC DEPENDENCY (CSD)
This section outlines the proposed methodology for extract-
ing semantic dependencies from microservice-based systems
and representing them in a semantic dependency matrix.
A. Methodology Overview
This methodology, called Component-based Semantic De-
pendency (CSD), aims to identify the semantic dependencies
between microservices within a system by focusing on the

semantics of architectural components and their communica-
tion flows. Its goal is to offer practitioners a holistic view
visualization that facilitates understanding of these semantic
relationships as the system evolves, ensuring maintainability
and consistency across different microservices in a system.
The CSD methodology builds on the concept of semantic
clones and similarities between CCGs. These CCGs represent
the system’s architectural components, including internal layer
calls, microservice endpoint calls, and interactions beyond
the system boundary [9]. The strength of the CSD method
lies in its ability to move beyond low-level syntactic code,
focusing instead on components interactions that span across
architectural layers. Considering the information in CCGs pro-
vides a semantic representation of the system’s execution flow,
capturing interactions between architectural components and
making it valuable for understanding the functional and com-
munication relationships within a specific slice of a project.
Our methodology, outlined in Figure 1, begins by analyzing
the system’s source code to construct CCGs for each mi-
croservice. Then, it measures semantic similarities between the
CCGs of different microservices. Finally, a heat map matrix
is utilized to visualize the detected semantic dependencies,
based on the similarities between the CCGs of each pair of
microservices in the system.
B. Component Call Graph (CCG) Construction (Phase 1)
Following the standard enterprise layered architecture, the
system architecture of each microservice project is divided
into components and layers communicating with each other
while preserving their single responsibility, such as Controller
(handling external communications through endpoints), Ser-
vice (containing business logic), and Data layer (managing
data storage) [9], [24]. The CCG captures all the necessary in-
formation to describe components’ properties and interactions
in such architecture, as highlighted in [9]. In this methodology,
the CCG serves as the granularity level for semantic com-
parisons. It is as an intermediate representation that shows
components’ properties, internal component layer calls, and
inter-service communications between microservices.
To construct CCGs from each microservice’s codebase,
we applied Software Architecture Reconstruction (SAR) [23],

[25], [26], a process that extracts system information to create
architectural views and analyze the system’s structure. For this
purpose, we developed a language-specific parser to extract the
necessary components and their properties for building CCGs,
in line with language standards. Our methodology classifies
components into four types: Controller, Service, Repository,
and Rest Call, each with specific properties, detailed in Table I.
Our SAR process involves three main steps. First, we
identify the layer-based components, such as Controller,
Service, and Repository. For example, In Java Spring,
these components are recognized through annotations like
@Controller, @Service, and @Repository. Second,
we extract the method definitions, including both the method
declarations and method bodies, within each component.
Third, starting from the top layer (Controller), we identify
the defined endpoint methods in each Controller component
(each of which serves as the starting point for a CCG)
and analyze their bodies to detect method calls to other
components such as service method call or endpoint call.
We use a signature matching technique to map the extracted
method calls to their corresponding method declarations. We
adopted a similar technique that arises in profiling systems
through log analysis, where the generated log lines match the
corresponding log statements in the source code [27]. Our
signature matching method extracts code call statements and
builds templates using regular expressions to match parameter
types with their corresponding in method declarations.

It is important to note that this phase of constructing
CCGs can adopt various approaches to achieve language-
agnostic capabilities, as demonstrated in [24]. However, this
methodology prioritizes the use of a language-specific parser
to ensure a more comprehensive extraction of information,
rather than generalizing across multiple languages, which is
not the primary focus of this methodology.
For example, as shown in Listing 1, an endpoint method
create in the TripController calls the save method in the
TripService, which then invokes both the endpoint /props and
the save method in TripRepository. These calls are detected,
formulated, and represented in a CCG as illustrated in Fig-
ure 2. The CCG starts at the controller, the service’s endpoint
interface, and traces through each method, mapping the entire
flow across the architectural layers.
C. Semantic Similarity Vectorization of CCGs (Phase 2)
This phase involves calculating the semantic similarity
between each pair of CCGs from different microservices and
generating a semantic similarity vector for each pair. As
shown in Table I, each component in a CCG has its own set
of properties. To determine the semantic similarity between
components across different CCGs, we compare each property
of a component with the corresponding property in the other
component. Various methodologies are applied to compare
these properties, and a similarity score is calculated.
In comparing method names we utilize a semantic name
comparator based on the WordNet project [28]. Using the
WordNet project allows us to not only compare syntactic
spellings of words to see if they are the same word but also to
move beyond their spelling into the semantic meaning of the
word. Using semantics allows us to apply our method more
generically and regardless of the authors we will be able to
find methods whose names describe the same functionality.
Semantic word comparison can also be applied to the argument
names, and names of custom types.
Next, we consider data type comparisons which are seen in
the return type and arguments properties. Within data types,
there are two options: built-in data types (e.g., String, int)
or custom data (e.g., class, struct) types. Built-in data types
have always the same name and contain the same type of
data so a simple syntactic approach can be utilized to find
their similarity. For custom data types, a similar semantic
approach used for method names can be implemented. We
can start by comparing the variable names of the declared
custom types, as well as the names of the custom data types
themselves. We can then dive deeper, comparing the names
of the variables within the data type. For instance, classes
are built primarily using built-in data types so these can be
syntactically compared. We can also compare the names of
values within a struct to see if they are semantically the same.
In instances where the number of variables in a custom data
type does not match, the method takes the highest similarity
score between combinations of matching between the two
custom data types. The final calculated similarity value is the
average between all similarity scores for all data types within
the specified property. Building on calculating the similarities,
we use syntactic comparisons to find similarities between
HTTP methods and URLs. For the HTTP method , an exact
literal match is necessary as there are only so many HTTP
methods, each performing a different function, so if the HTTP
method names do not match then the calls do not perform the
same semantic function. In terms of the URL it can be broken
down on the addresses each call travels to and the parameters
inserted into the URL. The URLs are compared to each other
syntactically, because if a URL goes to a different part of a
service than another they will have different URLs, and if the
services perform the same semantic function they will have
the same parameter types inserted into the call.
The final property to compare is the database operation ,
which is a simple logical matching. If a CCG pair compares

a delete with an insert method call, analyzing the query is un-
necessary since these functions have entirely different database
outcomes. An exception to the literal matching rule occurs as
insert and update operations often share semantic effects. In
some frameworks, like Spring, a single method may handle
both adding a new record (if it doesn’t exist) and updating
an existing one. Therefore, we treat them as equivalent in our
calculations. After calculating property similarities for each
CCG pair, we generate a vector representing their component
similarity scores, as shown in Figure 3.
D. Semantic Dependency Detection (Phase 3)
This phase aims to detect which pairs of CCGs are seman-
tically similar enough to indicate cloned semantics between
the participating microservices. By utilizing the calculated
similarity score vectors from each pair of CCGs, we can
analyze them with machine learning classification models to
determine whether the similarity vector is sufficiently close
to classify the CCGs as semantic clones. If so, we infer that
the two microservices containing these CCGs have a semantic
dependency. Machine learning is ideal for adapting to the
complexity of the patterns and the relationships between CCGs
that traditional methods may miss. It offers scalability for large
microservices, improving over time with new data.
With the potential availability of labeled data for CCG
pairs, we propose applying supervised machine learning to
predict whether two CCGs are similar enough to be considered
clones based on their calculated property similarity vector.
These properties carry semantic meaning for the respective
CCGs and components, making a simple linear model, such
as a logistic regression classifier [29], [30], suitable for cap-
turing this relationship. It is further validated through cross-
validation [31] with other models (i.e., decision trees, support
vector machines, and random forests). The logistic regression
model is effective and robust, particularly when working with
limited tabular data, as in this case. It aligns with our approach
by calculating the probability based on the various properties
of the similarity vector, thus indicating whether there is a high
likelihood that the CCG pair shares similar semantics. It is a
parametric model that attempts to learn the following function:
f(x) =P[y = +1| x] (1)
where x is the similarity vector, and y is a binary target with
y=1 meaning the CCGs pair is semantically similar and y=0
meaning the CCGs are not semantically similar. The goal is
to use supervised learning to satisfy equation 1 by finding a
set of coefficients in the following equation:
h(x) =θ(wT x + b) (2)
where w are the coefficients (a vector of scalar weights), b ∈ R
is the bias term, and θ is the logistic function defined as:
θ(z) = 1
1 + exp(−z), z ∈ R (3)
The model weights and bias terms are adjusted utilizing the
gradient descent method [29], which aims to minimize the
in-sample error rate. Logistic regression models at their core
cannot directly tell us whether two CCGs are semantically
similar or not, but will rather tell us based on the different
properties of the similarity vector if there is a high probability
of them being similar [30]. The machine learning algorithm
assigns weights to similarity scores’ properties based on their
importance, setting a threshold to classify CCG pairs as
semantically similar or not based on the probability.
E. Semantic Dependency Matrix Generation (Phase 4)
This phase tracks each pair of microservices and counts
how many CCG pairs were identified as semantically similar
in the previous stage. For example, if two microservices have
three different pairs of CCGs classified as semantically similar,
we consider these two microservices to have a semantic
dependency with a degree of three.
To represent and visualize the dependencies between each
pair of microservices, we employ a heatmap approach, as rec-
ommended in [16], [17]. We convert the semantic dependency
pairs into a grid, where each microservice with a dependency
is represented as both a row and a column. Each cell in the
grid contains the total number of CCGs that exhibit semantic
similarity between the two corresponding microservices. The
cell color becomes darker as the number of dependencies
increases between the pair of microservices.
It is important to note that the semantic dependency is con-
sidered bi-directional. This means that if Microservice A has a
semantic dependency with Microservice B, then Microservice
B also has a semantic dependency with Microservice A,
reflecting the mutual nature of their interactions.
IV. C ASE STUDY
In this section, we evaluate our proposed method using
an established benchmark. Using the CSD methodology, we
have analyzed an existing microservices-based system to iden-
tify semantic dependencies. The semantic interdependencies
among the microservices are illustrated in a corresponding
Semantic Dependency Matrix.
Our study emphasizes that the Semantic Dependency Matrix
serves as a valuable instrument for tracking semantic depen-
dencies among microservices within a system. Furthermore,
reanalyzing the system and regenerating the Semantic Depen-
dency Matrix enables developers to track dependencies in real-
time as they write code. Each new change in the source code
can be evaluated for semantic dependencies to identify any
new dependencies that are introduced or any violations that
may lead to inconsistencies between microservices.
A. Experimental setup
The experimental setup includes the selection of the bench-
mark, the data prepared for the execution and as a baseline, and
the implementation details of the prototype. A reproducible
package containing this produced data and prototype imple-
mentation have been published online in the dataset 1.
1) Benchmark: We conducted a pilot validation using a
subset of projects from the microservice dataset [32]. Among
them, TrainTicket2, recognized as the largest and most well-
established open-source benchmark for microservices, was
selected for this case study. It consists of 41 microservices built
using Java in Spring Boot framework and MySQL database.
2) Dataset Preparation: The dataset used in this study was
derived from the TrainTicket benchmark. Our methodology
was applied to extract the CCGs. To identify clone relation-
ships between each CCG pair, a semi-automated approach
was employed: a machine learning-based model was used
to pre-classify and label CCG pairs as potential clones or
non-clones based on structural and semantic features. These
classifications were subsequently validated through selective
manual inspection to ensure accuracy and reliability. The date
labels underwent an additional level of manual validation to
ensure thorough reasoning and accuracy in the results. To
mitigate bias, the manual validation of clone pairs and the
initial code analysis were performed by separate authors. The
dataset consists of 27,221 unique entry points, representing
distinct pairs of CCGs across 238 components distributed
over 41 microservices. Of these, 64 CCGs exhibited clone
relationships, while 174 did not. The semi-automated method
identified 32 clone pairs within the cloned CCGs, enhancing
scalability while maintaining rigorous validation standards.
3) Prototype Implementation: We developed a prototype as
a proof of concept for our CSD methodology. The prototype
comprises four key components that correspond to the phases
of the methodology: CCG Construction (Phase 1): This com-
ponent performs a source code analysis of an enterprise Java
application. We employed Java-specific tools, including the
Java Reflection library and Javassist [33], to statically analyze
our benchmark and construct the CCGs among its source code.
The benchmark utilizes the Java Spring framework, which
employs annotations such as @Controller, @RestController
1Reproducible Package: https://zenodo.org/records/13927257
2TrainTicket: github.com/FudanSELab/train-ticket/releases/tag/v0.1.0
for controllers, @Repository for repositories, and @Service
for services. It also employs RestTemplate for making remote
calls including the inter-service calls between microservices.
We extracted these components from the source code.
Semantic Similarity Vectorization of CCGs (Phase 2): In
this phase, the prototype calculates the semantic similarity
between properties of the components in the CCGs. It assesses
the semantic meaning of each property as detailed in the
methodology description. The prototype uses the WS4J project
and WordNet [28] to measure the semantic meaning difference
between words to allow us to compare properties, such as
method names. Following the comparison, we generate a
similarity vector for each pair of constructed CCGs from
different microservices.
Semantic Dependency Detection (Phase 3): The prototype
implements a logistic regression model using the scikit-learn
library [34] in Python. We train this model on the generated
training dataset and then it test and execute the model on the
benchmark data. The model identifies whether a pair of CCGs
is semantically similar, thereby determining the semantic de-
pendencies between the corresponding microservices.
Semantic Dependency Matrix Generation (Phase 4): Using the
classified similarities from the machine learning model, we
compile a list of microservices that exhibit semantic depen-
dencies and quantify the number of CCGs they share. We then
create a heat map to visualize the semantic dependency matrix
for our benchmark, with darker colors in the cells indicating
a higher number of shared CCGs between the services.
B. Results
This section presents the results obtained from each phase of
the methodology when executing the implemented prototype
on the selected benchmark.
1) CCG Construction (Phase 1): The first phase of our
methodology extracted and constructed 238 CCGs from the
source code, matching the manually generated CCGs in the
dataset. These CCGs were distributed across the microservices,
with the ts-admin-basic-info-service
microservice containing the highest number at 21
CCGs. On the lower end, ts-preserve-service,
ts-preserve-other-service, and
ts-verification-code-service each had 2 CCGs.
The most common number of CCGs per microservice was 6,
observed in 7 different microservices.
2) Semantic Similarity Vectorization of CCG (Phase 2):
This phase utilized the constructed CCGs from all microser-
vices in the system, generating 27,221 distinct pairs of CCGs
across different microservices. The proposed vectorization
methodology was then applied to the properties of each CCG
pair. This process produced a vector of 13 values for each pair,
corresponding to the properties listed in Table I. These values
represent the similarity degree for each of those respective
properties within each CCG pair.
3) Semantic Dependency Detection (Phase 3): We applied
the logistic regression model on the generated similarity
vectors, as detailed in the methodology. Given the imbalance
in the dataset, a weighted version of the logistic regression
model was utilized to emphasize accurate classification of the
undersampled (clone) class while reducing the weight for the
oversampled class (non-clone). The prediction threshold was
set at 0.99, which optimized the F1 score for the dataset [35].
In machine learning, this threshold value is often referred to
as a hyperparameter and is typically determined using cross-
validation techniques [36]. However, due to the limited data,
particularly the scarcity of clone samples in this dataset, cross-
validation was not feasible in this case study.
The model processed the generated 27,221 similarity vec-
tors, each representing a unique CCG pair. The predicted
classifications were compared with the actual labels from the
labeled dataset. As shown in Figure 4, out of 32 actual clone
pairs, the model correctly identified 24. However, 3 pairs were
falsely classified as non-clones when they should have been la-
beled as clones based on manual analysis. Additionally, 8 pairs
were incorrectly classified as clones. Upon re-examination, 6
of those 8 pairs were found to be true clones that had been
mislabeled during manual analysis, highlighting the model’s
ability to uncover mistakes in the dataset by learning the
component properties.
The three false negatives (semantic clones missed by
the model) likely resulted from dissimilar semantics, de-
spite the components performing the same function. In
these cases, comparisons involved a REST call versus a
repository call performing the same operation. For exam-
ple, one false negative compared a repository call to delete
a contact in ts-contacts-service with a REST call
in ts-admin-basic-info-service that performed an
identical function.
*: Upon re-examination, 6 of those 8 pairs were found to be true clones that had been
mislabeled during manual analysis.
Fig. 4: Confusion Matrix for the clones classification in
TrainTicket. (Top left is true negatives, top right is false positives,
bottom left is false negatives, and bottom right is true positives).
Metrics Analysis. The performance of the model on the
dataset is summarized in Table II, detailing key metrics
including accuracy, balanced accuracy, precision, recall, and
the F1 score [35], [37]. Upon analyzing the model’s perfor-
mance, we found it achieved a very high accuracy rate, with
most examples correctly classified. However, this metric is
somewhat misleading due to the dataset’s imbalance. A more
reliable measure is the balanced accuracy, which accounts for
this imbalance and stands at 94.4%. The model’s precision of
75% demonstrates that, out of every four examples predicted
as clones, one is likely a non-clone. Meanwhile, the high recall
indicates that the model is effective at identifying most existing
clones. Since the recall is less than 1, it’s expected that some
actual clones may be misclassified as non-clones. Lastly, the
F1 score, which combines precision and recall, confirms the
model’s overall performance.

Weights Analysis. The logistic regression model generates
weight values that indicate the importance of various features
in the prediction process. These weight values, which reflect
how much each feature contributes to the model’s decision-
making, are presented in Table III.
Analyzing these weights shows that the controller method
name, the return type of the controller method, and the return
type of the service emerged as the most influential factors in
the model’s predictions. This emphasizes that these particular
features play a critical role in determining the semantic simi-
larities between components in the microservices architecture.

4) Semantic Dependency Matrix Generation (Phase 4):
The Semantic Dependency Matrix (Figure 5) provides a de-
tailed overview of the dependencies between microservices
based on their shared CCGs. In this matrix, the microservice
names are listed both along the left side and across the top.
The intersection of each pair of microservices indicates the
degree of semantic dependency, represented by the number of
CCGs they have in common. Only microservices that share at
least one dependency with another are included in the matrix.
For each microservice, the total number of CCGs it contains
is indicated in parentheses next to its name. The color coding
in the matrix visually reflects the strength of these dependen-
cies: darker shades represent a higher number of shared CCGs
between two microservices, while lighter shades indicate fewer
commonalities. This matrix offers a clear, comparative view of
the semantic relationships across the system, making it easier
to identify how tightly coupled microservices are based on
shared functionalities.
The matrix highlights that the pair of microservices
that share the most semantic dependencies (15 CCGs) are
Fig. 5: Semantic Dependency Matrix of TrainTicket. (The
number in parentheses represents the total number of CCGs in each
microservice).
ts-order-other-service and ts-order-service.
Based on the names, the services appear to be performing
very similar if not identical functionality, so it is reasonable
for many of the semantic dependencies to be found in these
services. The semantic dependency in the code for these
microservices is due to multiple components in the code -
each service has an API route to get the price of an order
that has the same parameters, same return type, and a slight
change in the route URL. They also each contain a class to
call their respective API route, and these two classes share
the same logic except in a few places (database used, class
name, and logging information). They each contain a method
to access their respective repositories as well. The pair of
microservices that share the second most number (11 CCGs)
of semantic dependencies are ts-travel-service and
ts-travel2-service. These services also share similar
API routes, database schema, and other code fragments.
Based on these results, it is crucial to exercise caution when
modifying one service in a pair that shares significant semantic
dependencies. Changing one service without updating the
other can introduce errors that may propagate through the
system, affecting even unrelated services. Additionally, this
can lead to inconsistencies in business logic across workflows,
making it difficult to detect and trace the root cause of such
issues. These types of problems can be costly in terms of
time, money, and effort to identify and maintain. However,
the Semantic Dependency Matrix provides an instrument to
depict this perspective in a holistic view. It highlights these
hidden dependencies, helping prevent these costly mistakes.

A knowledge-based approach for guided development of
Infrastructure as Code
Zoe Vasileiou 1 · Indika Kumara 2 · Georgios Meditskos 1 · Kamil Tokmakov 4 · Dragan Radolovi´c5 ·
